summary: Specifies the Active Users service, which sends a list of the currently active users on the host without regard to the input. It is an Internet Standard for hosts that choose to implement it.

plainLanguage.summary: This document defines a service you can contact to find out who is currently logged in on a computer. It sends back a plain list of names, one per line, no matter what you send it.

subtitle: A service on port 11 that lists who is currently logged in to a host.

tldr.problem: Engineers want a simple way to ask a remote host which users are logged in, as a debugging and measurement aid.
tldr.mechanism: A server on port 11 sends a list of the currently active users, over TCP in a connection it then closes, or in one or more UDP datagrams. Any data received is ignored.
tldr.outcome: It is an Internet Standard for hosts that choose to implement it, and the list has no required syntax beyond putting each user on its own line.

today: RFC 866 is an Internet Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: An Active Users Service
sections.content:
RFC 866 defines the Active Users service and calls it a useful debugging and measurement tool. It simply sends a list of the currently active users on the host without regard to the input.

An active user is one who is logged in, such as listed in SYSTAT or WHO. Hosts on the ARPA Internet that choose to implement an Active Users Protocol are expected to adopt and implement this standard.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a service that reports the names of everyone logged in, whatever you ask it. That makes it handy for checking a remote machine.

sections.title: The TCP and UDP Services
sections.content:
Over TCP, a server listens on TCP port 11. Once a connection is established, a list of the currently active users is sent out the connection, any data received is thrown away, and the service closes the connection after sending the list.

Over UDP, a server listens on UDP port 11 and answers each received datagram with a datagram containing the list, ignoring the data it received. If the list does not fit in one datagram, the server sends a sequence of datagrams but must not break the information for one user, that is one line, across a datagram. The user side should wait for a timeout for all the datagrams to arrive, and they are not necessarily in order.
sections.plainLanguage: If the list is too long for one message, the server sends several. Each name stays whole in one message, and the messages may arrive out of order.

sections.title: User List Syntax
sections.content: There is no specific syntax for the user list. The RFC recommends that it be limited to the ASCII printing characters, space, carriage return and line feed, and that each user be listed on a separate line.
sections.plainLanguage: The reply is plain text with one person per line, like a sign-in sheet.

references.text: Postel, J., "Transmission Control Protocol", STD 7, RFC 793, September 1981.
